blocks.content: If you have already studied thread safety, you know that a lock (mutex) solves one specific problem: making sure only one thread touches a piece of shared data at a time.
Synchronization is the bigger toolbox this lesson is about the set of tools that let threads coordinate with each other, not just take turns.

Coordination means things like: "wait until there is something for me to do," "let at most 5 of you run at once," or "nobody moves to the next stage until everyone has finished this one." A plain lock cannot express any of those.
1. What is Synchronization?

Synchronization is the process of coordinating multiple threads so that shared resources are accessed in a safe and predictable manner. It ensures that only the appropriate threads can access or modify shared data at a given time, preventing race conditions, data corruption, and inconsistent results.
Synchronization controls how threads interact with shared resources, ensuring that concurrent operations produce correct and deterministic outcomes even when multiple threads execute simultaneously.
2. Why a lock by itself is not enough
blocks.text: 2. Why a lock by itself is not enough

blocks.content: A lock guarantees mutual exclusion: only one thread is inside the protected section at a time. But a lock has no concept of waiting for a condition. Imagine a shared to-do list between two threads one thread adds tasks, the other removes and processes them.
The processing thread needs to do nothing when the list is empty, rather than constantly opening the list, finding it empty, closing it, and checking again a moment later.

That repeated checking is called busy-waiting, and it is wasteful: the CPU spins doing pointless work instead of sitting idle, and it also adds delay, because the checking thread might not glance at the list at exactly the moment a new task arrives.

What is actually needed is a way for a thread to say "put me to sleep, and wake me up specifically when there is a task to process" and that is precisely what a condition variable provides. This is the first and most important idea in this lesson, so it gets the most detailed treatment.
3. Condition variables

A condition variable lets a thread sleep until a specific condition becomes true. While waiting, it automatically releases the lock so other threads can make progress. When another thread updates the shared state, it sends a signal, waking the waiting thread, which re-acquires the lock and checks the condition again.

A real-world analogy. Picture a single fitting room at a clothing store with one staff member holding the key (that's the mutex only one customer is ever inside). 

A customer who wants to try on clothes but finds the room occupied does not stand there yanking the door handle every second (that would be busy-waiting). 

Instead, they give their name to the staff member and sit down in the waiting area (that's calling wait on the condition variable) and they hand back any claim on the room while they wait. 

When the current customer leaves and unlocks the door, the staff member calls the next name (that's signal) and that customer gets the key and re-enters.

blocks.content: 4. How a Condition Variable Works

["Step 1: A thread acquires the mutex (lock).
","Step 2: The thread checks whether the required condition is true (for example, whether the queue contains data).
","Step 3: If the condition is not satisfied, the thread calls wait().
","Step 4: wait() atomically releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep.
","Step 5: Another thread acquires the mutex and modifies the shared state (for example, adds an item to the queue).
","Step 6: After updating the state, that thread calls signal() (or notify()).
","Step 7: The sleeping thread is awakened.
","Step 8: Before continuing, the awakened thread must re-acquire the mutex.
","Step 9: Once the mutex is acquired, the thread checks the condition again.
","Step 10: If the condition is now true, the thread continues its work.
","Step 11: If the condition is still false, the thread goes back to waiting.
"]
items: Step 1: A thread acquires the mutex (lock).
Step 2: The thread checks whether the required condition is true (for example, whether the queue contains data).
Step 3: If the condition is not satisfied, the thread calls wait().
Step 4: wait() atomically releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep.
Step 5: Another thread acquires the mutex and modifies the shared state (for example, adds an item to the queue).
Step 6: After updating the state, that thread calls signal() (or notify()).
Step 7: The sleeping thread is awakened.
Step 8: Before continuing, the awakened thread must re-acquire the mutex.
Step 9: Once the mutex is acquired, the thread checks the condition again.
Step 10: If the condition is now true, the thread continues its work.
Step 11: If the condition is still false, the thread goes back to waiting.

blocks.content: This process ensures that threads sleep efficiently while waiting for a state change and wake up safely when another thread signals that progress can be made.
5. Why Re-check After Waking Up?
blocks.text: 5. Why Re-check After Waking Up?

blocks.content: A thread should never assume that waking up means the condition is now true. After waking up, it must always check the condition again before proceeding.
Scenario A: Spurious Wakeup
Sometimes the operating system can wake a thread even though no signal() or notify() was sent.
This is called a spurious wakeup. When the thread checks the condition again, it may find that nothing has changed and simply go back to waiting.
Scenario B: Stolen Wakeup
Imagine two consumer threads are waiting for an item in a queue. A producer adds one item and sends a signal. Both consumers wake up and compete for the lock.

The first consumer acquires the lock, takes the only item, and releases the lock. When the second consumer finally gets the lock, it finds the queue empty again. Without re-checking the condition, it would proceed incorrectly.
6. Producer-Consumer Pattern

The Producer-Consumer pattern is used when one or more producer threads generate data and one or more consumer threads process that data. Both communicate through a shared buffer. Producers must wait when the buffer is full, and consumers must wait when the buffer is empty.
Producer Flow (put())

["Step 1: Acquire the Lock: The producer acquires the lock before accessing the shared buffer.
","Step 2: Check if the Buffer is Full: The producer checks whether the queue has reached its maximum capacity.
","Step 3: Wait if Full: If the buffer is full, the producer goes to sleep and releases the lock until space becomes available.
","Step 4: Add the Item: Once space is available, the producer adds the item to the queue.
","Step 5: Notify a Consumer: The producer signals notEmpty to wake up a consumer waiting for data.
","Step 6: Release the Lock: The producer releases the lock and finishes its work.
"]

Step 2: Check if the Buffer is Full: The producer checks whether the queue has reached its maximum capacity.
Step 3: Wait if Full: If the buffer is full, the producer goes to sleep and releases the lock until space becomes available.
Step 4: Add the Item: Once space is available, the producer adds the item to the queue.
Step 5: Notify a Consumer: The producer signals notEmpty to wake up a consumer waiting for data.

blocks.content: Consumer Flow (take())

["Step 1: Acquire the Lock: The consumer acquires the lock before accessing the shared buffer.
","Step 2: Check if the Buffer is Empty: The consumer checks whether there is any item available in the queue.
","Step 3: Wait if Empty: If the buffer is empty, the consumer goes to sleep and releases the lock until an item arrives.
","Step 4: Remove the Item: Once an item is available, the consumer removes it from the queue.
","Step 5: Notify a Producer: The consumer signals notFull to wake up a producer waiting for free space.
","Step 6: Release the Lock: The consumer releases the lock and returns the item.
"]
items: Step 1: Acquire the Lock: The consumer acquires the lock before accessing the shared buffer.
Step 2: Check if the Buffer is Empty: The consumer checks whether there is any item available in the queue.
Step 3: Wait if Empty: If the buffer is empty, the consumer goes to sleep and releases the lock until an item arrives.
Step 4: Remove the Item: Once an item is available, the consumer removes it from the queue.
Step 5: Notify a Producer: The consumer signals notFull to wake up a producer waiting for free space.
Step 6: Release the Lock: The consumer releases the lock and returns the item.

codes.python:
import threading
from collections import deque


class BoundedBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.queue = deque()
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.not_full = threading.Condition(self.lock)
        self.not_empty = threading.Condition(self.lock)

    def put(self, item):
        with self.not_full:                        # step 1: acquire the lock
            while len(self.queue) == self.capacity:  # step 2: check condition
                self.not_full.wait()                 # step 2b: release lock + sleep, as ONE action
            # step 5: re-check happens because this is a while, not an if
            self.queue.append(item)                  # condition true, safe to proceed
            self.not_empty.notify()                  # step 3: wake a sleeping consumer

    def take(self):
        with self.not_empty:
            while not self.queue:
                self.not_empty.wait()
            item = self.queue.popleft()
            self.not_full.notify()                   # wake a sleeping producer
            return item


if __name__ == "__main__":
    buffer = BoundedBuffer(2)

    buffer.put(1)
    buffer.put(2)
    print("Buffer filled with 2 items")

    print(f"Took: {buffer.take()}")
    print(f"Took: {buffer.take()}")

blocks.content: Why Use while Instead of if?
A thread may wake up even when the condition is still false. Therefore, after every wakeup, the thread must check the condition again.
Using while ensures the thread keeps waiting until the condition is actually satisfied, preventing synchronization bugs caused by spurious or stolen wakeups.

Real-World Analogy

Imagine a parking garage with 10 parking spots. Cars can enter as long as a spot is available. Once all 10 spots are occupied, any new car must wait outside until someone leaves. Every time a car exits, a spot becomes free and one waiting car can enter. A semaphore works in exactly the same way it controls access to a limited number of resources using a counter.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 7. What is a Semaphore?
A semaphore is a synchronization mechanism that controls access to a shared resource using a counter called permits.
Unlike a mutex, which allows only one thread at a time, a semaphore can allow multiple threads to proceed simultaneously up to a configured limit.
Each acquire() operation consumes a permit. If no permits are available, the thread waits. Each release() operation returns a permit and may wake a waiting thread.
Semaphore Example (3 Permits)

["Step 1: Initial State: The semaphore starts with 3 permits available.
","Step 2: Threads Acquire Permits
"]

Step 2: Threads Acquire Permits

blocks.content:
Thread A acquires a permit and starts running.
Thread B acquires a permit and starts running.
Thread C acquires a permit and starts running.

["Step 3: No Permits Left: All 3 permits are now in use, so the permit count becomes 0.
","Step 4: Another Thread Arrives: Thread D tries to acquire a permit but must wait because none are available.
","Step 5: A Permit is Released: Thread A finishes its work and releases its permit.
","Step 6: Waiting Thread Continues: The permit count becomes 1, Thread D wakes up, acquires the permit, and starts running.
"]

Step 4: Another Thread Arrives: Thread D tries to acquire a permit but must wait because none are available.
Step 5: A Permit is Released: Thread A finishes its work and releases its permit.
Step 6: Waiting Thread Continues: The permit count becomes 1, Thread D wakes up, acquires the permit, and starts running.

blocks.content: Connection Pool Example

["Step 1: Create a Semaphore with 10 Permits: The semaphore is initialized with 10 permits, representing 10 available database connections.
","Step 2: Request a Connection: When a thread calls acquire(), it consumes one permit.
","Step 3: Check Permit Availability: If permits are available, the thread gets a connection immediately. If all permits are in use, the thread waits.
","Step 4: Return the Connection: When the thread finishes using the connection, it calls release().
","Step 5: Wake Waiting Threads: The released permit becomes available again and a waiting thread can proceed.
"]

blocks.content: Semaphore vs Mutex
A mutex allows only one thread inside the critical section at a time and usually requires the same thread that acquired the lock to release it.
A semaphore uses a counter and does not track ownership. Any thread can release a permit, even if it was not the thread that acquired it.
Because of this, semaphores are ideal for controlling a fixed number of resources, such as database connections, API request limits, worker slots, or parking spaces.

Real-World Analogy

Imagine four students working on different sections of a group project. Even if three students finish early, they cannot start the presentation until the fourth student also finishes their part. Everyone waits at a common meeting point before moving to the next phase. This is exactly what a barrier does.

blocks.content: 8. What is a Barrier?

A barrier is a synchronization mechanism that forces multiple threads to wait until all participating threads reach the same point in execution. Once the last thread arrives, all waiting threads are released together and can continue to the next phase.
Barrier Flow

["Step 1: Start Phase 1: All worker threads begin their Phase 1 work independently.
","Step 2: Reach the Barrier: As each thread finishes Phase 1, it arrives at the barrier.
","Step 3: Wait for Others: Threads that arrive early must wait for the remaining threads.
","Step 4: Last Thread Arrives: When the final thread reaches the barrier, the waiting condition is satisfied.
","Step 5: Release Everyone: The barrier releases all waiting threads simultaneously.
","Step 6: Start Phase 2: All threads proceed to Phase 2 together.
"]
items: Step 1: Start Phase 1: All worker threads begin their Phase 1 work independently.
Step 2: Reach the Barrier: As each thread finishes Phase 1, it arrives at the barrier.
Step 3: Wait for Others: Threads that arrive early must wait for the remaining threads.
Step 4: Last Thread Arrives: When the final thread reaches the barrier, the waiting condition is satisfied.
Step 5: Release Everyone: The barrier releases all waiting threads simultaneously.
Step 6: Start Phase 2: All threads proceed to Phase 2 together.

["Step 1: Worker A, B, C, and D start Phase 1.
","Step 2: A, B, and C finish quickly and reach the barrier.
","Step 3: A, B, and C wait because D is still working.
","Step 4: D eventually finishes and reaches the barrier.
","Step 5: The barrier releases all four workers.
","Step 6: Phase 2 begins for everyone at the same time.
"]
items: Step 1: Worker A, B, C, and D start Phase 1.
Step 2: A, B, and C finish quickly and reach the barrier.
Step 3: A, B, and C wait because D is still working.
Step 4: D eventually finishes and reaches the barrier.
Step 5: The barrier releases all four workers.
Step 6: Phase 2 begins for everyone at the same time.

blocks.content: 9. What is a Monitor?
A monitor is not a new synchronization primitive. It is a design pattern that combines:
["Shared state","A mutex (lock)","Condition variables"]
items: Shared state
A mutex (lock)
Condition variables

blocks.content: into a single class.
The goal is to ensure that all access to shared data happens through methods that already handle synchronization correctly.
How a Monitor Works

["Step 1: Store the shared data inside a class.
","Step 2: Keep the lock and condition variables private.
","Step 3: Expose public methods such as put() and take().
","Step 4: Perform locking and unlocking inside those methods.
","Step 5: Prevent external code from directly accessing the shared state.
","Step 6: Guarantee thread safety through the class design itself.
"]
items: Step 1: Store the shared data inside a class.
Step 2: Keep the lock and condition variables private.
Step 3: Expose public methods such as put() and take().
Step 4: Perform locking and unlocking inside those methods.
Step 5: Prevent external code from directly accessing the shared state.
Step 6: Guarantee thread safety through the class design itself.

blocks.content: Example: Bounded Buffer
The BoundedBuffer class is a monitor because it contains:
["The shared queue","The lock protecting the queue","The condition variables used for waiting"]

The lock protecting the queue
The condition variables used for waiting

blocks.content: Clients simply call put() and take() without worrying about locks. The monitor hides the synchronization details and ensures the shared data is accessed safely.
10. Picking the right tool

["Mutex: You need exactly one rule: only one thread touches this data at a time. No waiting for a condition, no counting, no phases. The simplest and most common need.
","Condition variable: A thread needs to go to sleep until some specific fact about shared state becomes true buffer not empty, task finished, flag set and be woken efficiently rather than polling.
","Semaphore: You need to allow up to N things at once, not just one a pool of resources, a concurrency limit or you need one thread to signal another without an ownership relationship between them.
","Barrier: A fixed group of threads must all complete the current phase before any of them is allowed to start the next phase. Common in parallel simulations and batch processing pipelines.
","Monitor: Not a separate primitive a way of packaging a mutex and its condition variables together with the data they protect, so every caller is forced through correct synchronization automatically.
"]
items: Mutex: You need exactly one rule: only one thread touches this data at a time. No waiting for a condition, no counting, no phases. The simplest and most common need.
Condition variable: A thread needs to go to sleep until some specific fact about shared state becomes true buffer not empty, task finished, flag set and be woken efficiently rather than polling.
Semaphore: You need to allow up to N things at once, not just one a pool of resources, a concurrency limit or you need one thread to signal another without an ownership relationship between them.
Barrier: A fixed group of threads must all complete the current phase before any of them is allowed to start the next phase. Common in parallel simulations and batch processing pipelines.
Monitor: Not a separate primitive a way of packaging a mutex and its condition variables together with the data they protect, so every caller is forced through correct synchronization automatically.

blocks.content: 11. Common mistakes
Mistake 1: Using if Instead of while
A thread can wake up even when the condition is still false. Using if checks the condition only once, while while keeps checking until the condition is actually true.
Mistake 2: Signalling Before Updating State
Always update the shared state before calling signal() or notify(). Otherwise, a waking thread may not see the expected change and go back to sleep.
Mistake 3: Unbalanced acquire() and release()
Every acquire() must have a matching release(). Missing a release can block all future threads, while extra releases can allow more access than intended.
Mistake 4: Using signal() Instead of notifyAll()
If multiple threads are waiting for different conditions, waking only one thread may wake the wrong one. Use notifyAll()when multiple waiters could be affected.
Mistake 5: Busy Waiting Instead of Using Condition Variables
Continuously checking a condition in a loop wastes CPU and adds unnecessary delays. Condition variables allow threads to sleep efficiently until the state actually changes.
12. Quick reference

["Mutex: One thread at a time. The foundation everything else in this lesson builds on top of.
","Condition variable: Sleep until a condition is true, paired with a mutex. Always re-check in a loop after waking never assume one wakeup means success.
","Semaphore: A counter with acquire/release. Bounds concurrency to N, or signals across threads with no ownership requirement.
","Barrier: All N threads block until all N arrive, then everyone is released together. For phase-based parallel work.
","Monitor: Shared state plus its lock plus its conditions, bundled in one class so every caller goes through correct synchronization automatically.
","Default approach: Start with a mutex. Add a condition variable the moment a thread needs to wait for a state change. Add a semaphore when bounding concurrency to more than one."]
items: Mutex: One thread at a time. The foundation everything else in this lesson builds on top of.
Condition variable: Sleep until a condition is true, paired with a mutex. Always re-check in a loop after waking never assume one wakeup means success.
Semaphore: A counter with acquire/release. Bounds concurrency to N, or signals across threads with no ownership requirement.
Barrier: All N threads block until all N arrive, then everyone is released together. For phase-based parallel work.
Monitor: Shared state plus its lock plus its conditions, bundled in one class so every caller goes through correct synchronization automatically.
Default approach: Start with a mutex. Add a condition variable the moment a thread needs to wait for a state change. Add a semaphore when bounding concurrency to more than one.
